newsitem.title: FRANCE: French growth near government minimum target - poll.
newsitem.headline: French growth near government minimum target - poll.

text.p: The French economy is expected to grow by 2.2 percent this year and this may be enough to keep unemployment from getting worse than current record levels, a Reuter poll of 23 economists published on Tuesday showed.

In the "fitness test" year for European monetary union, the general view is that the centre-right government will meet the goal of limiting the public deficit to the equivalent of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

Despite the recent U.S. interest rate rise, economists see the Bank of France making further tiny cuts in the key French intervention rate, but its room for manoeuvre, while nurturing a strong currency tied to the mark, is seen as extremely limited and very much in the hands of Germany's Bundesbank.

With France's intervention rate currently just 10 basis points higher than Germany's equivalent "repo rate" of 3.0 percent, the margin is slim and even if the independent central bank closes the gap, economists see French interest rates turning upwards once again from the start of next year.

The survey, conducted between April 2 and April 8, produced a median, or midpoint, estimate of 2.2 percent GDP growth this year, just shy of an official 2.3 percent growth forecast which the government now describes as a minimum forecast.
The median forecast for 1998 is for 2.6 percent growth.
The U.S. dollar's rise in recent months to the highest level in years against the franc has brought with it the prospect of higher French growth through greater export competitiveness.

But many economists, and probably the government itself, are holding back from bullish estimates of the "windfall" value and waiting to see how the exchange rate between the two currencies evolves in the longer term.

Marie Owens-Thomsen at BIP Dresdner bank said the "dollar effect" would be limited in 1997 but that if the dollar stayed around current levels -- close to 5.8 francs per dollar -- to the end of the year, this could add 0.2 percent to GDP growth forecasts.
France's economic fortunes at the moment depend more on what is going on in Germany and beyond, however, and some analysts say GDP forecasting is currently extremely tricky.

Patrick Mange at Deutsche bank said he was sticking by his below-average forecast of 2.1 percent growth next year and that, in addition to various opinions on the way the dollar would go, it was hard to predict when important elements such as business investment or stock-building could kick in.
"We have more difficulty when the indicators are mixed, but when you have mixed indicators, it can be a sign of cyclical change, or upturn," Mange said.

He noted that 1994 produced growth of 2.5 percent but that people had not been counting on half that much early in the year, before a surge in producer prices, business investment and inventory changes.

A government report published this month also said the main risk to an otherwise rosy growth picture was if the U.S. economy does not slow down as expected, leading to further rate rises there and similar pressures in Europe.

On the jobs front there are some, albeit minimal, signs that economists felt the unemployment rate has peaked, at 12.8 percent. Latest government data showed 3.09 million unemployed in France at the end of February.
The latest Reuter poll gave a median prediction of 12.8 percent unemployment until the fourth quarter of this year, when it would start edging down slightly.
